documents.unit: Office of Faculty Development / Center for Teaching, Learning, and Development
documents.title: AI in the Syllabus
documents.summary: A Teaching and Learning page that advises instructors to write and discuss an AI syllabus statement and argues against blanket bans because detectors are unreliable. It offers four sample statements, from open use with required acknowledgement to default prohibition to authorization-only, and leaves the choice to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no university rule; it says "Rather than all out prohibiting AI usage" and offers sample statements ranging from "encourages and embraces" AI to "not to be used to complete work", with the choice left to each instructor, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The overview says to write "a clear AI statement and discussing it with students on the first day of class"; it directs instructors to communicate expectations at course start, so P09 (statement in the syllabus) fits best; the discussion element is P66 below.
units.anchor: producing a clear AI statement and discussing it with students on the first day of
units.policy: Instructors produce a clear AI statement and discuss it with students on the first day of class or in the introductory module of an asynchronous course.
units.fit_note: Recommends producing a clear statement and also discussing it with students; the page does not itself make the statement mandatory.

units.why: The page says "students who take more than one course in a semester stand a good chance of encountering different AI policies", a factual statement that rules vary by course, so it informs under P11 (a course's policy governs only that course).
units.anchor: students who take more than one course in a semester stand a good chance of
units.fit_note: Describes that policies differ across courses rather than stating that one course's rule does not carry over.

units.why: The overview calls maintaining academic integrity while balancing AI opportunities and challenges "essential and challenging", a framing statement of purpose and principle, so P56 (framework/preamble) rather than a rule.
units.anchor: Maintaining academic integrity while balancing the opportunities and challenges inherent to AI usage is both
units.fit_note: A short framing sentence rather than a full institutional framework.

units.why: The page says detection is "nearly impossible" so AI use cannot be enforced "with any consistency or validity"; this states a limit on control, which P82 covers, rather than a detector rule (P39), which the next unit codes.
units.anchor: it is nearly impossible to detect, and therefore enforce, the use of AI with any

units.why: "Rigorous testing has shown that AI detectors are unreliable in most practical scenarios" says detectors cannot be trusted as proof; this is P39 (do not rely on detectors) stated as a fact, so modality informs.
units.anchor: AI detectors are unreliable in most practical scenarios

units.why: The page cites evidence that detectors are "biased against English language learners", a bias and equity harm of AI-related tools; P53 (bias and harms) fits better than P39 since the point is harm to a group of students.
units.anchor: AI detectors have also been shown to be biased against English language learners
units.fit_note: The bias is in detectors, not in generative AI itself.

units.why: The page warns a prohibitive stance "may be tempting" but is "problematic (and potentially unethical)" and may "hinder the development of skills"; it advises against blanket bans, so P02 (permit rather than ban by default) is nearest, but it stops short of mandating permission.
units.anchor: it may be tempting to take a prohibitive classroom policy stance against the use of
units.fit_note: Advises instructors against prohibiting AI; it does not state an allow-by-default rule for students.

units.why: The restrictions "may hinder the development of skills and behaviors needed to engage thoughtfully in an AI-integrated world" gives a future-readiness reason to avoid bans, so P44 (learning AI is a professional skill).
units.anchor: hinder the development of skills and behaviors needed to engage thoughtfully in an AI-integrated world

units.why: The page describes an approach of requiring "students who use AI to reflect on and cite their use of AI tools" instead of prohibiting; with a reflection and citation duty it is P24 (disclose with each submission).
units.anchor: require students who use AI to reflect on and cite their use of AI tools
units.policy: Educators can require students who use AI to reflect on and cite their use of AI tools, for example by sharing their process and citing the prompts used.
units.fit_note: Also includes reflection and sharing process and prompts (P26, P25); presented as one approach educators use, not as a rule.

units.why: The page admits prompt-citation "may already be somewhat outdated" because tools like "Help me write" and Copilot need no prompts; this is a limit on a disclosure practice, so P82 (AI use cannot be fully controlled or verified).
units.anchor: it may already be somewhat outdated
units.fit_note: Says prompt-based citation is losing relevance because AI is embedded in familiar tools, not that AI cannot be prevented.

units.why: The Mollick quotation says that when AI is built into familiar tools "adoption becomes simple"; this concerns AI embedded in everyday software, covered by P07, but it states a prediction and no rule, so it is informs.
units.anchor: when AI gets integrated into a familiar tool, adoption becomes simple
units.fit_note: A prediction about embedded AI features, not a rule on editors or IDEs.

units.why: The page says syllabus policies "should be being clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused"; these are principles for writing AI syllabus statements, and no existing type covers them.
units.anchor: AI syllabus policies should be being clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused
units.uncovered_note: Principles for how to write an AI syllabus statement: clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused.

units.why: The page says how, when and why AI may be used "may need to be an ongoing conversation between institutions, educators, and students"; this asks for continuing discussion of the rules with students, so P66 (explain and discuss).
units.anchor: may need to be an ongoing conversation between institutions, educators, and students
units.fit_note: Also implies that AI rules will change over time (P54).

units.why: The page notes that "some educators are choosing to have students collaborate on the development of AI policies for their courses"; this is P67 (co-create with students), a practice described, not required.
units.anchor: some educators are choosing to have students collaborate on the development of AI policies for

units.why: "when students have a voice in the development of a policy, they may be more likely to adhere to it" gives a reason for co-creating policy, a benefit claim, so it informs under P67 as a separate rationale unit.
units.anchor: when students have a voice in the development of a policy, they may be more

units.why: Example 1 says "We will use large language model AI, including ChatGPT-4o and DALL-E 2, to enhance our learning"; the sample statement builds AI use into the course, so P79 (AI use in coursework).
units.anchor: We will use large language model AI, including ChatGPT-4o and DALL-E 2, to enhance our
units.fit_note: Sample statement; AI use is a class activity rather than a requirement on each assignment.

units.why: Example 1 says "we will be transparent in our use of AI in the completion of any classroom tasks" in line with the Student Code of Conduct; a duty to be transparent about AI use is P24.
units.anchor: we will be transparent in our use of AI in the completion of any classroom

units.why: Example 1 gives "AI Citation Format: Title of AI Tool. Prompt or brief description of topic of search depending on tool. Date of creation."; naming the tool, prompt and date is P25.
units.anchor: Title of AI Tool. Prompt or brief description of topic of search depending on tool.

units.why: Example 1 says "we will spend some time early in the semester co-creating a class agreement on the use of AI tools"; a class agreement made with students is P67.
units.anchor: we will spend some time early in the semester co-creating a class agreement on the

units.why: The sample says "policies around the use of large language tools will vary among courses", the reason for the co-created agreement; it is a fact that rules differ per course, so P11, as informs.
units.anchor: policies around the use of large language tools will vary among courses
units.fit_note: States that policies vary among courses as a reason for a class agreement.

units.why: The agreement's goals include that everyone "has access to and understands how to use the tools"; access and understanding of tools for all is P51 (equitable access).
units.anchor: ensure that everyone has access to and understands how to use the tools
units.fit_note: Goal of the class agreement; no cost or alternative provisions are stated.

units.why: The agreement is meant to explain "why it is or isn't appropriate to use the tools for certain course tasks"; explaining the reasons behind rules to students is P66.
units.anchor: why it is or isn’t appropriate to use the tools for certain course tasks

units.why: "We will revisit the agreement, as needed, throughout the semester" says the course AI policy will be reviewed and revised, which is P54.
units.anchor: We will revisit the agreement, as needed, throughout the semester

units.why: Example 2 says "This course encourages and embraces the ethical use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)", a default that welcomes AI, so P02 and unit stance encourage.
units.anchor: This course encourages and embraces the ethical use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

units.why: "you will sometimes be required to incorporate AI tools in your work" makes AI use mandatory in some assignments, which is P79.
units.anchor: you will sometimes be required to incorporate AI tools in your work

units.why: Students are "encouraged, as it makes sense to you to do so, to use AI in the completion of assignments"; a general allowance with discretion, P02.
units.anchor: encouraged, as it makes sense to you to do so, to use AI in the

units.why: "It is your responsibility, however, to be transparent in that use" binds students to disclose AI use, P24.
units.anchor: It is your responsibility, however, to be transparent in that use

units.why: Students must "examine the inherent bias and limitations of the AI tools you use"; the duty to critically evaluate AI and its bias is P31 (verify AI output); considering effects on one's learning is secondary.
units.anchor: examine the inherent bias and limitations of the AI tools you use
units.fit_note: Asks students to examine tool bias and limitations and to consider implications for their own learning, not only to check output correctness.

units.why: "you are required to read and edit, thoroughly, your assignment submissions, particularly any items created using AI" requires students to review what they submit, making them responsible for it, P29 rather than P31 since it concerns ownership of the submission.
units.anchor: you are required to read and edit, thoroughly, your assignment submissions

units.why: "for every assignment in this course, to submit an 'AI Acknowledgement'" is a required statement with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: required, for every assignment in this course, to submit an “AI Acknowledgement”

units.why: The acknowledgement must be "150-300 word" and cover the tool, why it was used, how it was used and "a reflection on your experience using the tool"; the required content is mostly reflective, so P26 (reflections) rather than P25.
units.anchor: you will include a 150-300 word acknowledgment
units.policy: For every assignment submission, students include a 150-300 word acknowledgment that identifies the tool(s) used, explains why they used them, describes how they used them to manage assignment requirements, and reflects on what worked or didn't, the tool's limitations and potential biases.
units.fit_note: Combines tool identification (P25) with a reflection; no prompt or output is required.

units.why: Students who do not use AI should "highlight your non-AI approach and/or your reasons for deciding not to use certain tools" in the acknowledgement; this extends disclosure to non-use, which no type covers.
units.anchor: please use the “AI Acknowledgement” to highlight your non-AI approach
units.uncovered_note: Students who choose not to use AI use the acknowledgement to describe their non-AI approach or reasons.

units.why: The sample says the approach "will help us to develop our skills for using AI while maintaining our academic integrity"; a reason that learning to use AI is a skill alongside integrity, P44.
units.anchor: will help us to develop our skills for using AI while maintaining our academic integrity

units.why: Example 3: "Large-language, generative AI tools are not to be used to complete work for this course unless specifically directed to do so" bans AI by default unless the instructor directs, P01.
units.anchor: not to be used to complete work for this course unless specifically directed to do

units.why: "to be effective in your use of existing tools, you need to be skilled in your own right" gives the reason that foundational skills are the aim of the class, P41 (AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill).
units.anchor: you need to be skilled in your own right
units.fit_note: Also says work should demonstrate critical thinking and the student's own ideas.

units.why: "I ask you to embrace the challenge of thinking through and developing your responses to assignments without the support of AI" asks students to do the thinking themselves, P32 (student stays the primary problem-solver) over P19 since it is framed as a challenge to embrace.
units.anchor: embrace the challenge of thinking through and developing your responses to assignments without the support

units.why: "information about accessing and using specific tools for specific assignment components will be clearly outlined for you" says that where AI is used the instructor will specify tools and components; a per-assignment setting, P04.
units.anchor: information about accessing and using specific tools for specific assignment components will be clearly outlined
units.fit_note: Also commits the instructor to spell out access to and use of specific tools.

units.why: "Please let me know at any time if you have questions or concerns about the use of AI in this course" invites students to ask the instructor, P10.
units.anchor: Please let me know at any time if you have questions or concerns about the
units.fit_note: An invitation to raise questions or concerns, not specifically a duty to ask before using AI.

units.why: Example 4: "should only be used in this course when specifically authorized by the instructor" allows AI only with instructor authorization, P107 (prior approval) rather than P01 since authorization is the gate and the text says "should".
units.anchor: should only be used in this course when specifically authorized by the instructor
units.fit_note: Authorization is by the instructor; the text also names ChatGPT and Microsoft CoPilot.

units.why: "Use of such tools presents ethical and academic dishonesty issues, especially if the work is presented as your own" is a reason AI is risky for integrity, so P95 (fairness and honesty rationale).
units.anchor: Use of such tools presents ethical and academic dishonesty issues, especially if the work is

units.why: "you must be fully transparent with your use, including proper citation and any other documentation required by your instructor" is a required disclosure with citation, P24.
units.anchor: you must be fully transparent with your use, including proper citation and any other documentation

units.why: "Submitting work that is not your own without proper citation and using resources that are not authorized are both Academic Integrity violations" classes uncited and unauthorized use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: using resources that are not authorized are both Academic Integrity violations

units.why: "you are responsible for any incorrect/false information that is obtained using these tools, so be sure to double-check" tells students to verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: be sure to double-check any information or citations for accuracy before submitting any coursework
units.fit_note: Also makes the student responsible for false information obtained from the tools.

units.why: The page states Example 4 is "currently under review by the WMU Faculty Senate Professional Concerns Committee"; this says who is reviewing the suggested language, P84.
units.anchor: currently under review by the WMU Faculty Senate Professional Concerns Committee

units.why: The examples are offered as "examples of what policies that support that ongoing conversation might look like"; the page supplies sample syllabus language for instructors, P110.
units.anchor: Following are several examples of what policies that support that ongoing conversation might look like

documents.title: MOA 2514 revision: syllabus AI requirements
documents.summary: A signed Faculty Senate Memorandum of Action (MOA 25/14, March 2026) that adds a required AI statement to the list of syllabus elements. It leaves the substance of the rule to each instructor and ties violations to the Student Code's definition of cheating.
documents.stance_why: The policy says it requires faculty "to explicitly state how AI can and cannot be used in the classroom without dictating what that looks like for faculty", so it sets no AI stance of its own and hands the rule to instructors, which is delegates.

units.why: The recommendation says the councils "recommend the required inclusion of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Statement on all WMU syllabi", an AI statement in every syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: required inclusion of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Statement on all WMU syllabi

units.why: The syllabus element reads "The syllabus must make the expectations about AI use in the course explicit", binding instructors to state expectations in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: syllabus must make the expectations about AI use in the course explicit

units.why: The committees chose to "require faculty to explicitly state how AI can and cannot be used in the classroom without dictating what that looks like for faculty", so content is left to each instructor, P04.
units.anchor: without dictating what that looks like for faculty

units.why: The rationale says the subcommittee "met with university stakeholders and received feedback on sample statements from other universities", which describes how the policy was developed, P84.
units.anchor: met with university stakeholders and received feedback on sample state ments from other universities

units.why: The Student Code defines cheating as using technology that has not been authorized, and the policy says AI counts as "other technology," "but only if faculty are explicit"; the fallback depends on instructor explicitness, so P06 (rule when syllabus is silent) is the nearest type.
units.anchor: but only if faculty are explicit about what is and is not authorized
units.fit_note: Says AI counts as unauthorized technology only if the faculty are explicit; does not set a default ban or default permission when the syllabus is silent.

units.why: "instructors should explicitly outline whether, and in what ways, AI tools may be used in their course" tells instructors to state what is allowed, P09.
units.anchor: instructors should explicitly outline whether, and in what ways, AI tools may be used in

units.why: "Students are expected to follow the specific expectations outlined by the instructor" makes students follow each instructor's AI rules, P78.
units.anchor: Students are expected to follow the specific expectations outlined by the instructor

units.why: Students are to "use any approved tools transparently and with proper acknowledgment", a disclosure duty for approved AI use, P24.
units.anchor: use any approved tools transparently and with proper acknowledgment

units.why: "Using AI tools in ways not permitted for an assignment, or failing to disclose their use when required, may be considered a violation of the University's academic integrity policy" classes misuse as misconduct, P36; nondisclosure (P28) is the lesser part.
units.anchor: failing to disclose their use when required, may be considered a violation of the University’s
units.fit_note: Also makes failure to disclose when required a possible violation (P28).

units.why: The responsible offices are listed as the Academic and Informational Technology Council, Professional Concerns Committee, Faculty Senate Executive Board and College Deans, naming who owns and enforces the policy, P80.
units.anchor: Academic and Informational Technology Council,

units.why: "Proposed date of next review: September 2029" sets a review cycle for the syllabus policy, P54.
units.anchor: Proposed date of next review: September 2029

units.why: The related guidelines say the Center for Teaching and Learning "maintains resources for faculty on the use of AI in the classroom, including guidance on developing course policies", supporting faculty, P63 over P115 as the resources help faculty develop policy.
units.anchor: maintains resources for faculty on the use of AI in the classroom, including guidance on
units.fit_note: Also directs readers to a web page of guidance (P115).

units.why: The rationale states the committees "were charged by the Faculty Senate Executive Board to create a syllabus statement pertaining to the use of AI", describing who initiated the policy, P84.
units.anchor: charged by the Faculty Senate Executive Board to create a syllabus statement pertaining to the

notes: Example statements on the AI in the Syllabus page are coded as units because they state policy text, but they are samples for instructors, not WMU rules. No school or computing-unit policy found.
